div.head: VII Atr 1.2
div.ab: Hoc est ut detur de omni carruca denarius uel denarii ualens.
Hoc est ut detur de omni carruca denarius vel denarii valens.
Hoc est ut detur de omni carruca denarius vel denarii valens.
Nämlich von jedem Pfluge [Landes] gebe man einen Pfennig oder Pfennigs Werth.
Namely, from every plough[land] let a penny or a penny's worth be given.
From every plough-land a penny or the value of a penny shall be given.
Thus, a penny or the value of a penny is to be given from every plowland.
div.note: Hoc est ut: et ut Br; hoc ut Hk

note.seg: Et ut Br; Hoc ut Hk
Et ut Br; Hoc ut Hk
Nichts mit Pflugalmosen (u. 7) oder (wie Schmid meint, den Steenstrup Normannerne III 370 korrigiert) dem Peterspfennig hat diese Zahlung an die Kirche zur einmaligen Landesbusse zu tun
This payment to the Church for a single penance of the whole land has nothing to do with plough-alms (below 7) or (as Schmid supposes, corrected by Steenstrup Normannerne III 370) with Peter’s Pence

æt sylh (suluh; Var. sulhgange) peninc bewahrt aus Original Hom. n. Wulfstan 170. 173; vgl. æt þære sylh: de omni caruca II As 16. Wo er das Werkzeug ‘Pflug’ meint, setzt Q nicht carruca (s. d. Wb). Möglicherweise lag Q und Hom. ein Exemplar für Kent vor; vgl. Gl Hufe 11. 3ff.—Dagegen hid steht dafür in VIIa Atr 2, 2

æt sylh (suluh; var. sulhgange) peninc is preserved from the original in Hom. n. Wulfstan 170. 173; cf. æt þære sylh: de omni caruca II As 16. Where Q means the implement ‘plough’, he does not use carruca (see that word in Wb). Possibly Q and the Hom. had before them a copy for Kent; cf. Gl Hufe 11. 3ff.—On the other hand, hid stands for it in VIIa Atr 2, 2

‘oder vom Kopf 1 Pfennig’ fügt hinzu Hom. 170, ‘oder ein geschmiertes Brot vom rauchenden Herde’ 170. 173; vgl. Gl Kopfsteuer. De bordariis habet rex scotum de suo capite tantum; Domesday I 173; II 106. Dantes capitularia aurum atque argentum übs. falsch der Prediger um 1025 (bei M. Förster in Morsbach Festschr. 117), der also Kopfsteuer nicht versteht

‘or 1 penny per head’ is added by Hom. 170, and ‘or a buttered loaf from each smoking hearth’ by 170. 173; cf. Gl Kopfsteuer. De bordariis habet rex scotum de suo capite tantum; Domesday I 173; II 106. The preacher of c. 1025 (in M. Förster in Morsbach Festschr. 117) mistranslates Dantes capitularia aurum atque argentum, and so does not understand poll-tax

The same phrase occurs in II As. 16 Q where the original is æt þære sylh, cf. Wulfstan, pp. 170, 173. The A.S. text has hide. Liebermann suggests that the use of the term carruca (i.e. sylh) may be due to Kentish usage but it is possible that sulh may have been in general use popularly. A parallel expression is found in Norse, e.g. Egilssaga, Chap. 52: skilling silfrs af plógi hverjum.

Cf. Wulfstan, loc. cit.: swa gesyfledne hlaf æt hreocendum heorðe, swa elles hwæt, swa witan þonne to ðearfe gerædan hwilum be teoðunge, hwilum be mannes efenwihte, hwilum be freotmen, hwilum an, hwilum oðer.
